claim: Eco1 acetyltransferase acetylates the Smc3 cohesin subunit in meiotic S phase to establish chromatin boundaries, independently of DNA replication.
source: Eco1 acetylates the Smc3 cohesin subunit in meiotic S phase to establish chromatin boundaries, independently of DNA replication.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and related figures.

claim: Boundary formation by Eco1 is critical for prophase exit and for the maintenance of cohesion until meiosis II.
source: Boundary formation by Eco1 is critical for prophase exit and for the maintenance of cohesion until meiosis II, but is independent of the ability of Eco1 to antagonize the cohesin release factor, Wpl1.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 8 and 9 showing prophase exit defects and meiosis II segregation defects in eco1-aa cells.

claim: Prevention of cohesin release by Wpl1 is essential for centromeric cohesion, kinetochore mono-orientation, and co-segregation of sister chromatids in meiosis I.
source: Conversely, prevention of cohesin release by Wpl1 is essential for centromeric cohesion, kinetochore mono-orientation, and co-segregation of sister chromatids in meiosis I.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2 and Figure 8 showing that deletion of WPL1 rescues centromeric cohesion and meiosis I segregation defects in eco1-aa cells.

claim: Cohesin organizes the genome by forming intra-chromosomal loops and inter-sister chromatid linkages.
source: Cohesin organizes the genome by forming intra-chromosomal loops and inter-sister chromatid linkages.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established scientific knowledge supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: During gamete formation by meiosis, chromosomes are reshaped to support crossover recombination and two consecutive rounds of chromosome segregation.
source: During gamete formation by meiosis, chromosomes are reshaped to support crossover recombination and two consecutive rounds of chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge about meiosis.

claim: Eco1 levels increased after meiotic entry, were maximal around the time of meiotic S phase, and declined after DNA replication.
source: Eco1 levels increased after meiotic entry, were maximal around the time of meiotic S phase, and declined after DNA replication
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Smc3-K112,K113 acetylation accumulated after Eco1 appearance, persisted throughout the meiotic divisions, and declined during meiosis II.
source: while Smc3-K112,K113 acetylation (henceforth Smc3-Ac), detected using a verified antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C), accumulated after Eco1 appearance, persisted throughout the meiotic divisions, and declined during meiosis II (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data in Figure 1C.

claim: In cdc6-md and clb5Δ clb6Δ meiotic cells, Smc3-Ac appeared with comparable timing to wild type and was only modestly reduced.
source: In cdc6-md and clb5Δ clb6Δ meiotic cells, Smc3-Ac appeared with comparable timing to wild type and was only modestly reduced (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data in Figure 1E and quantification in Figure 1F.

claim: Smc3-Ac was greatly diminished in cells lacking the meiotic cohesin kleisin subunit (rec8Δ).
source: In contrast, Smc3-Ac was greatly diminished in cells lacking the meiotic cohesin kleisin subunit (rec8Δ) (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data in Figure 1E and quantification in Figure 1F.

claim: Cohesin acetylation on its Smc3 subunit during meiotic S phase occurs independently of DNA replication and programmed double-strand break formation.
source: We conclude that cohesin acetylation on its Smc3 subunit during meiotic S phase occurs independently of DNA replication and programmed double-strand break formation.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the data from Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Eco1 is essential for vegetative growth and eco1Δ viability is restored by deletion of WPL1 (eco1Δ wpl1Δ cells).
source: Eco1 is essential for vegetative growth and eco1Δ viability is restored by deletion of WPL1 (eco1Δ wpl1Δ cells) (Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Growth of ECO1-FRB-GFP cells was inhibited in the presence of rapamycin, but restored by deletion of WPL1.
source: Growth of ECO1-FRB-GFP cells was inhibited in the presence of rapamycin, but restored by deletion of WPL1 (Figure 1H), consistent with successful anchor-away (Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2008; Sutani et al., 2009; Unal et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1H showing growth on plates with and without rapamycin.

claim: Upon induction of meiosis in the presence of rapamycin, Smc3-Ac was undetectable in ECO1-FRB-GFP cells and full-length Rec8 persisted long after its expected time of degradation.
source: Upon induction of meiosis in the presence of rapamycin, Smc3-Ac was undetectable in ECO1-FRB-GFP cells and full-length Rec8 persisted long after its expected time of degradation (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data in Figure 1I.

claim: Only a minor fraction of ECO1-FRB-GFP cells completed the first meiotic division.
source: Furthermore, only a minor fraction of ECO1-FRB-GFP cells completed the first meiotic division (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by nuclear division data in Figure 1J.

claim: Eco1 is required for efficient meiotic division.
source: We conclude that Eco1 acetylates Smc3 on residues K112,113 during S phase of meiosis, and that Eco1 is required for efficient meiotic division.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the data from Figure 1.

claim: Deletion of WPL1 did not restore nuclei division to eco1-aa cells.
source: Consistently, WPL1 deletion did not restore nuclei division to eco1-aa cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Eco1 is essential for meiosis, even in the absence of Wpl1.
source: Therefore, in contrast to vegetative cells, Eco1 is essential for meiosis, even in the absence of Wpl1.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the data from Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deletion of WPL1 restored cohesion at the centromere (CEN5-GFP), but not at the chromosomal arm site (LYS2-GFP) in eco1-aa cells.
source: Remarkably, we observed distinct effects of WPL1 deletion in eco1-aa cells on centromeres and chromosome arms: deletion of WPL1 restored cohesion at the centromere (CEN5-GFP), but not at the chromosomal arm site (LYS2-GFP) (Figure 2F and H).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by GFP foci separation data in Figure 2F and H.

claim: A critical role of Eco1 in cohesion establishment at centromeres is to counteract Wpl1, while on chromosome arms Eco1 plays an additional, essential function.
source: We conclude that a critical role of Eco1 in cohesion establishment at centromeres is to counteract Wpl1, while on chromosome arms Eco1 plays an additional, essential function.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the data from Figure 2F and H showing differential effects of WPL1 deletion on centromeric versus arm cohesion in eco1-aa cells.

claim: Calibrated ChIP-seq revealed a global increase in the levels of the cohesin subunit Smc3 on chromosomes of wpl1Δ prophase I cells.
source: Calibrated ChIP-seq revealed a global increase in the levels of the cohesin subunit Smc3 on chromosomes of wpl1Δ prophase I cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by ChIP-seq data in Figure 3A.

claim: Chromosomal Smc3 was greatly reduced in eco1-aa genome-wide, with the exception of core centromeres, where cohesin levels were less affected.
source: In contrast, chromosomal Smc3 was greatly reduced in eco1-aa genome-wide, with the exception of core centromeres, where cohesin levels were less affected (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by ChIP-seq data in Figure 3D.

claim: Inactivation of Wpl1 increased the chromosomal levels of Smc3 in eco1-aa, and this was particularly apparent at centromeres.
source: Interestingly, inactivation of Wpl1 increased the chromosomal levels of Smc3 in eco1-aa, and this was particularly apparent at centromeres, where Smc3 levels in eco1-aa wpl1Δ were comparable to the wpl1Δ mutant alone (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by ChIP-seq data in Figure 3D.

claim: The function of Eco1 at pericentromere borders and chromosome arms in meiotic prophase is twofold: Eco1 protects cohesin from Wpl1-dependent removal and Eco1 has an additional, Wpl1-independent function in cohesin retention at border and arm sites.
source: Taken together, our Rec8 and Smc3 ChIP-seq show that the function of Eco1 at pericentromere borders and chromosome arms in meiotic prophase is twofold. First, Eco1 protects cohesin from Wpl1-dependent removal since cohesin levels are higher in eco1-aa wpl1Δ compared to eco1-aa cells. Second, Eco1 has an additional, Wpl1-independent function in cohesin retention at border and arm sites because cohesin levels are higher in wpl1Δ compared to eco1-aa wpl1Δ cells.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the ChIP-seq data from Figure 3.

claim: Analysis of contact probability on chromosome arms as a function of genomic distance revealed an increase in long-range interactions in both eco1-aa and wpl1Δ mutants, which was further exacerbated in eco1-aa wpl1Δ cells.
source: Analysis of contact probability on chromosome arms as a function of genomic distance revealed an increase in long-range interactions in both eco1-aa and wpl1Δ mutants, which was further exacerbated in eco1-aa wpl1Δ cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Hi-C data in Figure 4C.

claim: Loop size increased from ~10 kb in wild type to ~20 kb in eco1-aa or wpl1Δ cells and up to ~40 kb in eco1-aa wpl1Δ.
source: This indicated an increase in loop size from ~10 kb in wild type to ~20 kb in eco1-aa or wpl1Δ cells and up to ~40 kb in eco1-aa wpl1Δ (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Hi-C data analysis in Figure 4C.

claim: Spots and stripes on the Hi-C contact maps were stronger and increased in number in wpl1Δ, but were more diffuse in eco1-aa, even after WPL1 deletion.
source: Further inspection revealed that spots and stripes on the Hi-C contact maps, indicative of positioned loops anchored on two or one sides, respectively, were stronger and increased in number in wpl1Δ, but were more diffuse in eco1-aa, even after WPL1 deletion (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Hi-C contact maps in Figure 4D.

claim: The absence of active Eco1 reduced insulation across centromeres.
source: In contrast, the absence of active Eco1 reduced insulation across centromeres (Figure 5A; see also top-right and bottom-left quadrants on the ratio difference maps in Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Hi-C pileup data in Figure 5A and ratio maps in Figure 5B.

claim: Boundaries at pericentromere borders were barely detectable in eco1-aa and were only partially rescued by deletion of WPL1.
source: In contrast, boundaries at pericentromere borders were barely detectable in eco1-aa and were only partially rescued by deletion of WPL1 (Figure 5C and D), suggesting that Eco1 is critical to halt loop extrusion at borders, even in the absence of Wpl1.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Hi-C pileup data in Figure 5C and ratio maps in Figure 5D.

claim: Wpl1 and Eco1 limit loop expansion through distinct mechanisms in meiotic prophase: Wpl1 destabilizes loop-extruding cohesin to reduce its lifetime, while Eco1 anchors cohesin at boundary sites to stabilize and position loops.
source: These data indicate that Wpl1 and Eco1 limit loop expansion through distinct mechanisms in meiotic prophase. While Wpl1 destabilizes loop-extruding cohesin to reduce its lifetime, Eco1 anchors cohesin at boundary sites to stabilize and position loops.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the Hi-C data from Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Eco1-dependent loop stabilization critically defines the boundaries that demarcate the pericentromeric domain.
source: We further note that Eco1-dependent loop stabilization critically defines the boundaries that demarcate the pericentromeric domain.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the Hi-C data from Figure 5.

claim: Long-range contacts, loops, and loop boundaries arise between early G1 and prophase also in clb5Δ clb6Δ cells, though at lower levels compared to wild type.
source: Long-range contacts, loops, and loop boundaries arise between early G1 and prophase also in clb5Δ clb6Δ cells, though at lower levels compared to wild type (Figure 6E–I, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Hi-C data in Figure 6E–I and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: Loop extrusion and boundary establishment occur independently of DNA replication but DNA replication itself, or another S phase CDK-dependent process, boosts loop formation and anchoring.
source: Overall, these results indicate that loop extrusion and boundary establishment occur independently of DNA replication but that DNA replication itself, or another S phase CDK-dependent process, boosts loop formation and anchoring.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the Hi-C data from Figure 6 comparing wild-type and clb5Δ clb6Δ cells.

claim: Eco1 anchors cohesin at least in part independently of cohesion, that is, by acting directly on loop-extruding cohesin.
source: Therefore, Eco1 anchors cohesin at least in part independently of cohesion, that is, by acting directly on loop-extruding cohesin.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the ChIP-seq data from Figure 7—figure supplement 1 showing that Eco1 affects cohesin distribution in unreplicated cdc6-md cells.

claim: Eco1 directs the formation of cohesin-dependent boundaries and loop anchors in unreplicated cells.
source: The fact that formation of anchored loops in meiotic prophase I requires Eco1, but neither Cdc6 nor S phase CDKs leads to two conclusions. First, Eco1 directs the formation of cohesin-dependent boundaries and loop anchors in unreplicated cells.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the Hi-C data from Figure 7 comparing wild-type, eco1-aa, cdc6-md, and eco1-aa cdc6-md cells.

claim: Loop anchors are further focused and strengthened in the presence of a sister chromatid.
source: Second, loop anchors are further focused and strengthened in the presence of a sister chromatid.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the Hi-C data from Figure 7 comparing replicated and unreplicated cells.

claim: Eco1 is likely to promote loop anchoring through cohesion-dependent and -independent mechanisms, with the latter occurring via acetylation of loop-extruding cohesin.
source: Therefore, Eco1 is likely to promote loop anchoring through cohesion-dependent and -independent mechanisms, with the latter occurring via acetylation of loop-extruding cohesin.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the data from Figures 6 and 7.

claim: SPO11 deletion abolished the prophase exit delay of both eco1-aa and eco1-aa wpl1Δ cells.
source: Figure 8A shows that SPO11 deletion abolished the prophase exit delay of both eco1-aa and eco1-aa wpl1Δ cells, confirming that Eco1 is required for satisfaction of the recombination checkpoint to allow prophase exit.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 8A showing spindle pole body separation.

claim: In ~35% of spo11Δ eco1-aa cells, CEN5-GFP foci segregated to opposite poles in meiosis I ('equational segregation'), indicating that centromeric cohesion is required for the establishment of sister kinetochore mono-orientation.
source: However, in ~35% of spo11Δ eco1-aa cells, CEN5-GFP foci segregated to opposite poles in meiosis I ('equational segregation'), indicating that centromeric cohesion is required for the establishment of sister kinetochore mono-orientation (Figure 8C and E).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by live-cell imaging data in Figure 8C and E.

claim: Deletion of WPL1 largely rescued the equational segregation of spo11Δ eco1-aa cells in meiosis I.
source: Consistent with its ability to restore centromeric cohesion to eco1-aa cells (Figures 2F and 8D), deletion of WPL1 largely rescued the equational segregation of spo11Δ eco1-aa cells in meiosis I (Figure 8C and E).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by live-cell imaging data in Figure 8C and E.

claim: Eco1 antagonism of Wpl1 allows the establishment of centromeric cohesion to enable sister kinetochore mono-orientation.
source: This supports the idea that the establishment of sister kinetochore mono-orientation requires the formation of centromeric cohesion by Eco1. Therefore, Eco1 antagonism of Wpl1 allows the establishment of centromeric cohesion to enable sister kinetochore mono-orientation.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the data from Figure 8.

claim: Defective meiosis II segregation in eco1-aa cells is not rescued by deletion of WPL1, whether or not Spo11 is present.
source: Moreover, defective meiosis II segregation in eco1-aa cells is not rescued by deletion of WPL1, whether or not Spo11 is present (Figure 8F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by live-cell imaging data in Figure 8F.

claim: Eco1 is essential for chromosome segregation during meiosis II, even in the absence of Wpl1.
source: Therefore, Eco1 is essential for chromosome segregation during meiosis II, even in the absence of Wpl1.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the data from Figure 8F.

claim: Eco1 enables accurate meiosis II segregation by anchoring cohesin at chromatin boundaries to generate robust cohesion at pericentromere borders.
source: Since wpl1Δ rescues the loss of cohesin on pericentromeric borders in eco1-aa cells, but not the anchoring of loops, it is likely that Eco1 enables accurate meiosis II segregation by anchoring cohesin at chromatin boundaries to generate robust cohesion at pericentromere borders.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the data from Figures 3, 5, and 8.

claim: Smc3-Ac is essential for meiosis.
source: Ectopic SMC3 expression rescued the inviability of smc3-md spores while smc3-K112,113R expression did not, indicating that Smc3-Ac is essential for meiosis (Figure 9—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by spore viability data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Like eco1-aa, smc3-K112,113R reduced chromosomal cohesin levels genome-wide, but had a milder effect at centromeres.
source: Like eco1-aa (Figure 3A–D), smc3-K112,113R reduced chromosomal cohesin levels genome-wide, but had a milder effect at centromeres (Figure 9C and D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by ChIP-seq data in Figure 9C and D.

claim: WPL1 deletion increased Smc3 levels in smc3-K112,113R cells, but to a lesser extent than in the eco1-aa background.
source: WPL1 deletion increased Smc3 levels in smc3-K112,113R cells (Figure 9C and D), but to a lesser extent than in the eco1-aa background (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by ChIP-seq data in Figure 9C and D compared to Figure 3A.

claim: Like Eco1, Smc3-Ac is more important for retention of cohesin at pericentromere borders and arm sites than at centromeres.
source: Therefore, like Eco1, Smc3-Ac is more important for retention of cohesin at pericentromere borders and arm sites than at centromeres, suggesting a role in boundary formation.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the ChIP-seq data from Figure 9C and D.

claim: Smc3-Ac is required to ensure co-segregation of sister chromatids in meiosis I and accurate meiosis II chromosome segregation.
source: In the case of smc3-K112,113R, but not smc3-md, this equational meiosis I segregation was rescued by deletion of WPL1 (Figure 9F). Sister chromatid segregation during meiosis II was also greatly impaired in both smc3-md and smc3-K112,113R cells, but in neither case was it rescued by WPL1 deletion (Figure 9G, Figure 9—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by live-cell imaging data in Figure 9F and G.

claim: Eco1-dependent Smc3-Ac functionally organizes meiotic chromosomes for their segregation.
source: We conclude that Eco1-dependent Smc3-Ac functionally organizes meiotic chromosomes for their segregation.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the data from Figure 9.

claim: At centromeres, Eco1-dependent Smc3 acetylation counteracts Wpl1 to direct sister kinetochore mono-orientation and thereby enforce sister chromatid co-segregation in meiosis I.
source: At centromeres, Eco1-dependent Smc3 acetylation counteracts Wpl1 to direct sister kinetochore mono-orientation and thereby enforce sister chromatid co-segregation in meiosis I.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the data from Figures 8 and 9.

claim: Eco1 acetylation of Smc3 is essential for prophase exit and sister chromatid segregation in meiosis II, even in the absence of Wpl1, likely due to its requirement for cohesin anchoring to establish chromatin boundaries.
source: Eco1 acetylation of Smc3 is also essential for prophase exit and sister chromatid segregation in meiosis II, even in the absence of Wpl1, likely due to its requirement for cohesin anchoring to establish chromatin boundaries.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and is based on the data from Figures 8 and 9.

claim: The control of loop formation and cohesion establishment by Eco1 and Wpl1 allows centromeres, pericentromeres, and chromosome arms to adopt region-specific functions in sister kinetochore co-orientation, cohesion maintenance, and recombination.
source: We find that the control of loop formation and cohesion establishment by Eco1 and Wpl1 allows centromeres, pericentromeres, and chromosome arms to adopt region-specific functions in sister kinetochore co-orientation, cohesion maintenance, and recombination.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: During meiotic S phase, substantial Smc3 acetylation, and anchoring of chromatin boundaries, occurs even in the absence of DNA replication.
source: In mitotically dividing yeast cells, Smc3 acetylation is largely coupled to DNA replication (Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2008); however, during meiotic S phase, substantial Smc3 acetylation, and anchoring of chromatin boundaries, occurs even in the absence of DNA replication.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figures 1, 6, and 7.

claim: Smc3-Ac can exist independently of cohesion establishment.
source: Therefore, Smc3-Ac can exist independently of cohesion establishment.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data showing Smc3 acetylation in unreplicated cells.

claim: Eco1 and Smc3-Ac confer a more fundamental role in chromosomal loop positioning that is indispensable for meiosis.
source: In addition to Wpl1 antagonism, Eco1 and Smc3-Ac confer a more fundamental role in chromosomal loop positioning that we find to be indispensable for meiosis.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figures 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9.

claim: A fraction of cohesin engaged in cis-looping is acetylated by Eco1, with two consequences: Smc3-Ac blocks cohesin's Wpl1-dependent release and Smc3-Ac anchors cohesin at the base of loops, preventing loop migration and restricting extrusion.
source: However, a fraction of cohesin engaged in cis-looping is acetylated by Eco1, with two consequences. First, Smc3-Ac blocks cohesin's Wpl1-dependent release. Second, Smc3-Ac anchors cohesin at the base of loops, preventing loop migration and restricting extrusion, resulting in the stable positioning of moderately sized loops.
evidence: This model is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: The absence of Wpl1 increases the lifetime of loop-extruding cohesin complexes, resulting in loop extension.
source: The absence of Wpl1 increases the lifetime of loop-extruding cohesin complexes, resulting in loop extension (Figure 4; Costantino et al., 2020; Dauban et al., 2020; Haarhuis et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by data in Figure 4 and citations to prior work.

claim: The combined absence of both Eco1 and Wpl1 results in mobile cohesin with extended lifetimes on chromosomes and untempered loop-extruding activity, leading to long, poorly positioned loops.
source: The combined absence of both Eco1 and Wpl1 results in mobile cohesin with extended lifetimes on chromosomes and untempered loop-extruding activity, leading to long, poorly positioned loops.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The role of Eco1 in anchoring cohesin is Wpl1 independent and is essential for meiosis.
source: Therefore, the role of Eco1 in anchoring cohesin is Wpl1 independent and is essential for meiosis.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figures 2, 8, and 9.

claim: The positioning activity of Eco1 also facilitates cohesion establishment along chromosome arms by anchoring cohesin complexes that are engaged in linking the two sister chromatids ('cohesive cohesin').
source: The positioning activity of Eco1 also facilitates cohesion establishment along chromosome arms by anchoring cohesin complexes that are engaged in linking the two sister chromatids ('cohesive cohesin').
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figures 2, 3, and 9.

claim: Loop boundaries are increased in focus in the presence of a sister chromatid, suggesting that cohesive cohesin complexes are also directly positioned by acetylation.
source: Our finding that the converse is also true, that is, that loop boundaries are increased in focus in the presence of a sister chromatid, together with the fact that functional pericentromeric cohesion in meiosis II also requires Eco1, suggests that cohesive cohesin complexes are also directly positioned by acetylation
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figures 6, 7, and 8.

claim: At centromeres, Smc3-Ac, which blocks the destabilizing activity of Wpl1, is sufficient for cohesion establishment, likely due to enhanced cohesin loading or specialized anchoring mechanisms at this site.
source: At centromeres, Smc3-Ac, which blocks the destabilizing activity of Wpl1, is sufficient for cohesion establishment, likely due to enhanced cohesin loading or specialized anchoring mechanisms at this site.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figures 2, 8, and 9.

claim: Eco1-dependent cohesin acetylation also establishes loop positioning in S phase of yeast mitotic growth.
source: A recent report indicates that Eco1-dependent Smc3 acetylation also establishes loop positioning in S phase of yeast mitotic growth (Bastié et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by a citation to a recent report.

claim: The residues acetylated by Eco1 are part of the surface that binds DNA in the cohesin 'clamp' structure.
source: However, recent reports investigating the relationship between molecular structure and loop-extruding activity of human cohesin identified the residues acetylated by Eco1 as part of the surface that binds DNA in the cohesin 'clamp' structure.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by citations to recent reports.

claim: Eco1 and Smc3-Ac are critical for the completion of meiotic recombination to allow exit from meiotic prophase.
source: We found that Eco1 and Smc3-Ac are critical for the completion of meiotic recombination to allow exit from meiotic prophase.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figures 8 and 9.

claim: Restoration of cohesin levels in Eco1-deficient cells by removal of Wpl1 was insufficient to support DNA repair and prophase exit, or for chromosomal arm cohesion.
source: Restoration of cohesin levels in Eco1-deficient cells by removal of Wpl1 was insufficient to support DNA repair and prophase exit, or for chromosomal arm cohesion.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figures 2 and 8.

claim: Loss of positioned chromatin loops causes defects in the repair of double-strand breaks, leading to a delay in prophase exit.
source: We speculate that loss of positioned chromatin loops causes defects in the repair of double-strand breaks, leading to a delay in prophase exit.
evidence: This speculation is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figure 8.

claim: Eco1 is present beyond S phase into prophase, suggesting that it may play an active role in loop repositioning and/or the anchoring of new loops during homologous recombination.
source: Eco1 is present beyond S phase into prophase, suggesting that it may play an active role in loop repositioning and/or the anchoring of new loops during homologous recombination.
evidence: This speculation is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figure 1C.

claim: The loss of centromeric cohesion in eco1-aa cells is accompanied by the aberrant segregation of sister chromatids to opposite poles in meiosis I, which was also rescued by Wpl1 inactivation.
source: Our live-cell imaging revealed that the loss of centromeric cohesion in eco1-aa cells is accompanied by the aberrant segregation of sister chromatids to opposite poles in meiosis I, which was also rescued by Wpl1 inactivation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figure 8.

claim: Acetylation of Smc3 by Eco1 counteracts Wpl1 at centromeres allowing the establishment of centromeric cohesion, which in turn facilitates kinetochore fusion via the monopolin complex.
source: Although we cannot currently rule out the possibility that Eco1 has an additional substrate that confers its function in sister kinetochore co-orientation as has been suggested for fission yeast (Kagami et al., 2017), the simplest explanation is that acetylation of Smc3 by Eco1 counteracts Wpl1 at centromeres allowing the establishment of centromeric cohesion, which in turn facilitates kinetochore fusion via the monopolin complex (reviewed in Duro and Marston, 2015).
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figures 2, 8, and 9, along with citations to prior work.

claim: During meiosis, cohesion on chromosome arms requires Eco1 and Smc3-Ac even in the absence of Wpl1.
source: During meiosis, cohesion on chromosome arms requires Eco1 and Smc3-Ac even in the absence of Wpl1.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figures 2 and 9.

claim: The ability of Eco1 to reinforce chromatin boundaries is critical for cohesion during meiosis.
source: This argues against the idea that the key function of Smc3-Ac in cohesion is to antagonize Wpl1. Instead, we propose that the ability of Eco1 to reinforce chromatin boundaries is critical for cohesion during meiosis.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figures 2, 3, 5, 8, and 9.

claim: Eco1 is required to retain cohesin at pericentromere borders and, consequently, to establish the boundaries that structure pericentromeres during meiosis.
source: We now show that Eco1 is required to retain cohesin at these sites and, consequently, to establish the boundaries that structure pericentromeres during meiosis.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data from Figures 3, 5, and 8.

claim: Sister chromatids undergo random meiosis II segregation in cells lacking Eco1, whether or not Wpl1 is present.
